The Discount Rate in Iranian Conditions
Why Not CAPM and Beta?
In textbooks: cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium.
On the Tehran Stock Exchange beta isn’t reliable: price limits, queues, trading halts and low float separate the daily price from value.
The build-up method is more honest.
The Build-up Method
Nominal risk-free rate: the yield to maturity of 2 to 3-year Akhza.
Equity risk premium: usually 5 to 10 percentage points; a judgement. Keep it the same for all companies.
Specific risk premium: 0 to 10 points for low liquidity, dependence on a government decision, heavy foreign-currency debt, weak governance.
Cost of debt = finance costs ÷ average borrowings. The tax shield only at the real effective rate.
WACC = equity weight × cost of equity + debt weight × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate)
Akhza 30%, equity risk premium 7, specific risk premium 3 points. Cost of equity?

That’s why the build-up method.

Nominal, Real and Terminal Value
Consistency Matters More than Precision
The most common error: nominal cash flow with a real rate, or the reverse.
Nominal: forecast with inflated prices and exchange rates, discount at a nominal rate (say 38%), terminal growth about long-term inflation.
Real (suggested to start): forecast at today’s prices, discount at a real rate. 38% nominal and 30% inflation → about 6.2%. Real terminal growth 0 to 2%.
The real method needs two adjustments: maintenance CAPEX at today’s prices, and the working-capital “inflation tax” ≈ inflation × (receivables − payables).
Terminal Value
In most models 70 to 85% of the total value comes from this one line.
Don’t take real terminal growth above 2%.
Convert the terminal value into an implied multiple (÷ last-year EBITDA) and compare it with peers.
Always write the terminal value’s share of the total next to the result.
Terminal value = cash flow in the year after the forecast period ÷ (discount rate − terminal growth)

Relative Multiples

EV = market value of equity + bank debt (foreign-currency at today’s rate) − free cash − non-operating investments + non-controlling interests (in consolidated). EBITDA = operating profit + depreciation.
5 steps: 4 to 6 similar peers; normalised profit and the same date; the median, not the mean; explain the differences; build a range.

An Integrated Financial Model in Excel
The FIS-valuation-model.xlsx File

The three financial statements for the next five years are linked, and the value per share comes out of that forecast. A hypothetical “Company D”, 200 thousand tonnes of sales. Amounts in million rials.

Sheets: Guide, Historical (fill in from Codal), Assumptions (scenario, inflation, tax, days, discount rate, multiples), Model (read only; balance check zero), Valuation (FCFF, WACC, TV, sensitivity, EV/EBITDA, range).
Colours: blue = input, black = formula, green = link from another sheet. Only change the blue ones.
How the Statements Connect
Net profit is added to equity and dividends are subtracted.
Receivables, inventory and payables are built from days; their increase is subtracted from cash.
Fixed assets = last year + CAPEX − depreciation.
The net change in cash builds the balance sheet cash; negative cash = a warning of a loan or capital increase.
Balance check = assets − (liabilities + equity); if it isn’t zero, something is wrong.
Five Lessons from Company D
Asymmetric risk: in the bad scenario (selling price 1% below inflation, feedstock 1% above inflation) the margin falls from 30 to 26% and value drops 54%.
Inflationary profit: the base margin rises from 30 to 35% because depreciation is historical; maintenance CAPEX at today’s prices (337,500 against depreciation of 250,000) takes it back.
Working-capital drag: CFO/NI is about 0.83 because inflation inflates receivables and inventory.
The tax exemption ends from year three: 15% to 25%.
Base DCF 2,984 against the median multiple’s 2,344; implied TV multiple 6.7×. Whenever two methods are far apart, find the reason; averaging is not a reason.
